39bdb9361a56de520bdb.summary: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse is the first Castlevania game since 2008. 18 years had to pass for a brand-new title in the series to come out. And no, I’m not counting Lords of Shadow . While I’m happy for those that enjoy the newest Castlevania romp, it’s not what I think about when I picture the series. If you were to ask me what defines a Castlevania game, I’d say it’s either the classic arcade-style original games, or the Koji Igarashi-led games. In the hypothetical sliding scale between Metroid and Castlevania , it seems like Belmont’s Curse veers closer to the former. In fact, I’d venture to say that there are too many Metroidvania games in the style of Metroid , and not nearly enough similar to the Igarashi-led Castlevania games. When I think of Metroidvania in the Castlevania “Igavania” style, I think of games like Ender Lilies and Ender Magnolia , Team Ladybug’s Record of Lodoss War: Deedlit in Wonder Labyrinth and Blade Chimera , and of course, Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night . I’m sure there are a few more, but even so, the list isn’t very long. What differentiates these games different from the likes of Hollow Knight or Blasphemous is a heavier emphasis on RPG elements, varied weapons and equipment, different spells and abilities, and a design ethos more focused on fighting hordes of enemies, rather than focusing on moment-to-moment, deliberate and challenging enemy encounters. Image via Konami By now it’s probably obvious that I gravitate towards the Castlevania side of things. However, I’ve officially run out of games in that style to play. I could boot up a plethora of other Metroidvania games, sure. But games that draw specifically from the style that originated with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night ? I’m afraid it’s looking dire. And I get it. What I’m asking for is a fundamentally different design style from what’s popular in the genre nowadays. The Igavania games are, usually, experiences where the player has a lot more control over the pacing of enemy encounters. It’s pretty easy to cheese through a Symphony of the Night or Bloodstained , get a particular weapon drop and start mowing down enemies. What’s more popular nowadays is the FromSoft style of challenge and curated fights. This style marries well with the non-linear exploration of the genre, but fundamentally changes how to approach combat and bosses, compared to how fast one can decimate bosses in Castlevania or adjacent games. Even the aforementioned Ender Lilies and Ender Magnolia are skirting the line between Igavania and Soulslike at times. The same goes for a lot of other side-scrolling action games, like Salt and Sanctuary , The Last Faith , or Mandragora: Whispers of the Witch Tree . While these are interesting games, it’s not exactly what I’m looking for in this space either. Even Metroid Dread boasts a parry and an increase in challenge compared to the rest of the series. e45d1c2f8fc9c018b23f.summary: During the early hours of Grand Theft Auto VI , I was walking near a bowling alley in an interstate area. Playing as Lucia, I overheard chatter about an ongoing drug operation inside. I desperately needed money, so I engaged in some tomfoolery. I took a shotgun from my car, approached the guard, and opened fire at their knees, taking them down without killing them. I took as much loot with me as I could from the wild shootout and eventually found a locked safe and some explosives nearby. You can imagine what I did next. It didn’t take long until the police surrounded the bowling alley. There was no easy way out. I had been greedy, took too long, and had to deal with my choices. As the police entered the building, another shootout between the gang members and the cops ensued. That was my cue. I climbed a ladder to the roof, jumped to the street, and drove an unlocked motorbike as fast as I could, hoping the cops wouldn’t recognize me. It was as if I had never been there, and I was a handful grand richer in GTA VI . This is just one example of the dozens of situations I got into over 83 hours in Leonida. However, if I told you that some of my other favorite moments in GTA VI involved setting up some drywall as Jason and moving a coffee table, you’d probably look at me funny. Grand Theft Auto VI is a game of contrasts. Image via Rockstar GTA VI shares a lot in common with Red Dead Redemption 2 , but it’s in how these two games differ that the former shines. While I appreciate RDR2 , it features a very stark divide between what you can do in its world with those systems and how the main story missions take place. GTA VI features bombastic set pieces, car pursuits, and scripted sequences aplenty, especially in the later chapters. The game suffers a bit as it moves into the second half, where these more linear missions and set pieces take place. Especially considering the length of it. But GTA VI also constantly required me to engage with the open world and these granular, interactive systems in order to advance the story. During one early story mission, Jason and Lucia need to rob a few stores to get some cash, but you don’t need to hit all of them. Which ones I robbed and how I went about it was all up to me. Some I managed to hit clean and fast, with the cops unable to track me. With others, I failed to find and eliminate CCTV recordings. I got in trouble with the law and had to skulk around the shadows, find the correct car to steal, and wait for an opportunity to approach the nearest clothing store to change my appearance. Images via Rockstar The usual freedom is also met with a level of friction and limitations that creates fascinating opportunities in GTA VI . During early hours, committing the titular “grand theft auto” isn’t easy and money is hard to come by. These limitations made me engage with systems that I’d otherwise not try, such as public transport and taxis, and I’d always make sure my car was in top shape and with a full tank. The aforementioned level of freedom extends to combat. My preferred method involved taking down enemies non-lethally, shooting at knees, hands, or elbows to disarm them.
